28. **(Added 2026-08-16, F4-3 — physical storage-deletion safety: evidence, idempotency and the tenant boundary. Additive runtime change; NO schema change, NO migration, NO production mutation.)** Baseline `origin/main` @ `fb22b94cf607c64fdb0e33ba98329018ef8c9f5e`, clean tree. **This task set no retention period, approved no deletion, opened no new deletion path and enabled no provider object-lock.** F4-3's hard rule — `NO PHYSICAL DELETION without approved legal/KVKK policy` — is intact and now **test-pinned**: `POST .../deletion-review/execute` still does not exist, `deletion-review` is still dry-run-only, `dataRetentionPolicy.ts`/`dataRetentionCleanupJob.ts` still perform no physical deletion, and no scheduled job deletes a clinical object on a timer. **The defect that was fixed is the opposite one — deletions that were already happening could not be proven and could not be recovered from.** The two paths that physically delete patient-uploaded bytes (`DELETE /api/patients/:patientId/attachments/:id`, `DELETE /api/lab-orders/:id/attachments/:attId`) deleted the DB row first — correct for attachments, where that `deleteMany` *is* the atomic legal-hold gate PR #163 introduced — then called `deleteFile(row.filePath)` with the error swallowed (`labOrders.ts` entirely; `attachments.ts` to `console.error` only). Because the deleted row was the **only** persisted home of the storage key, a failed storage deletion produced a permanently unreconcilable orphan: the object survived, nothing could ever name it again, no alert fired, and the caller was told the deletion succeeded. That is exactly the state F4-3's contract forbids ("DB says deleted, physical object still exists, no durable retry/evidence") and, under KVKK, an erasure claim the system cannot substantiate — the worse half of the failure, because a silent partial erasure is indistinguishable from a complete one. **A second, wider defect was found while proving the first:** `fileStorage.deleteFile` swallowed **every** local-mode `unlink` error, not only "already gone" — `EPERM`, `EACCES`, `EBUSY`, `EROFS` and I/O errors were all reported to **every caller in the repository** as a successful deletion, including `clinicBulkExportPackage.ts`, whose own comment stated the opposite ("`deleteFile` itself already swallows local-mode ENOENT, so this second check only matters for remote-storage errors"). Only `ENOENT` is idempotent by definition; the rest now propagate. **The contract now in force** lives in the new `server/src/services/storageObjectDeletion.ts` (`deleteStoredObjectWithEvidence`) and **invents no parallel system** — it reuses `writeAuditLogInTx` (the repository's existing **non-swallowing** audit writer) as the authoritative evidence ledger, `recordOperationalEvent` as **secondary** operator alerting only, and the same idempotency semantics already accepted for export artifacts (`deleteStorageObjectIdempotent`). It provides: a **fail-closed tenant boundary** — the key must be prefixed by the owning clinic's id under the F4-1A key contract, so a safe-form key belonging to another clinic is **refused** (`rejected_tenant_mismatch`, nothing deleted), closing the previously-unguarded case where a corrupted `filePath` on clinic A's row would have destroyed clinic B's object; **fail-closed key validation** (empty, traversal, UNC, drive-relative, control-character all refused, `rejected_unsafe_key`); **idempotency** where "already gone" is a terminal success and only a *tenant-scoped* key may be upgraded to `already_absent`, because `fileExists()` returns `false` for a legacy absolute path and would otherwise fabricate a success out of a real failure; **evidence on every outcome including refusals** (clinic, organization, entity type/id, action, `requestedAt`, `executedAt`, outcome, failure code, actor); the audit record being the artefact that still names the object after the row is gone, and therefore the reconciliation input for a leaked object; and **escalation** — every non-terminal outcome also writes an `OperationalEvent` (`error`, or `critical` when the evidence write itself did not commit), as a secondary signal that is never read back as proof the authoritative record was written. **No new PHI sink was created to achieve this:** a tenant-scoped key is server-generated and opaque so it is recorded verbatim, while a **legacy absolute path may embed the original file name** (routinely a patient's name in a dental clinic) and is therefore recorded only as a SHA-256 digest — no file name, patient name, TCKN, phone, email or DICOM metadata is written to prove a deletion, asserted by test. The lab-order attachment DB delete was additionally narrowed from an id-only `delete({ where: { id } })` to a conditional `deleteMany` scoped by `labWorkOrderId` + the order's own `clinicId`. **The DB-first ordering was deliberately preserved**, not "fixed": deleting the object first would move the legal-hold decision out of the `deleteMany` WHERE clause into a read-then-delete and reopen precisely the TOCTOU window PR #163 closed, so the residual risk is handled by evidence instead. **Two genuine schema gaps were found, reported and deliberately NOT implemented** (the task contract forbids creating a migration without program review): **`R-079`** — `LabOrderAttachment` has no `legalHold` column, so the lab-order attachment delete is the one attachment-delete path in the codebase with **no legal-hold gate at all** (the same gap F2-PREP-005 recorded as `IMG-13`); the proposed minimal additive migration mirrors `PatientAttachment` exactly and is the program owner's decision, not an agent's. **`R-080`** — there is no durable deletion intent and no automatic retry; a failed deletion is now evidenced and alerted but retrying it is an operator action, and reverse-orphan detection (object present, no DB row) still does not exist. **Two test defects were also fixed:** `kvkkAttachmentImagingLifecycle.test.ts`'s `getDeleteRouteBlock()` sliced a fixed 3500-character window that silently truncated the route once the evidence call was added, turning a real assertion into a false negative; and naive substring scans counted *comment prose* about `deleteFile` as live call sites. **Explicitly untouched:** F4-2/`R-030`/`R-030-DB`/`R-030-FILES`, F4-1A2 (including `labOrders.test.ts:283`'s pinned `buildStorageKey(order.clinicId` assertion), the imaging ingest rollback path inside the F2 port boundary, and the long-standing `ActivityLog` text that carries `originalName` (a product decision, not a fail-closed safety boundary — every **new** evidence record is filename-free). **Deleting a primary object does NOT delete it from backups** — pgBackRest repositories, `pg_dump` artifacts, `FileBackupRun` copies and any pre-deletion snapshot are unaffected and expire on their own separate, still-undecided retention schedules; this is stated explicitly in `docs/compliance/53-kvkk-attachment-imaging-lifecycle.md` §16A and no sentence of this item may be quoted as evidence that a subject's data has been erased everywhere. **Tests (all local, exit 0):** `test:storage-deletion-evidence` **33/33** (new; disposable fixture files only — no real patient attachment or imaging object touched), `test:kvkk-lifecycle` **111/111**, `test:lab-orders` **32/32**, `test:patient-privacy` **38/38**, `test:storage-key-contract` **41/41**, `test:clinic-bulk-export` **117/117**, `test:imaging` **103/103**, `test:data-retention` **43/43**, `test:dental-chart-clinic-scope` **17/17**, `test:orphan-file-inspection-log-privacy` **1/1**, server `npm run typecheck` exit 0, root `npm run log-privacy-guard:scan` exit 0 (268 files, no new violations), `git diff --check` exit 0. **Migration required: NO · Migration created: NO · Production migration: NO · Production mutation: NONE.** **F4 phase status stays `TODO`**; `R-030`/`R-030-DB`/`R-030-FILES` remain `OPEN`; `FIRST_CUSTOMER_RECOVERY_GATE = NOT_SATISFIED` — this task neither advances nor claims any part of that gate. Task status: `AGENT_COMPLETED` / `TESTS_PASSED` / `PR_OPENED` (draft) — `NOT_MERGED` / `NOT_DEPLOYED` / `NOT_PRODUCTION_VERIFIED`. **F4-3-R1 correction (2026-08-16, same task, same PR #430 — added after the architecture review of that PR):** the review correctly found that the safety claim above was **not yet guaranteed**. The first implementation wrote its evidence through `writeAuditLog` and `recordOperationalEvent`, and **both of those are documented fire-and-forget writers that swallow their own persistence failures**, so this sequence remained reachable: DB row deleted -> physical storage deletion fails -> audit write fails and is swallowed -> operational event write fails and is swallowed -> the caller sees `failed` (i.e. "tracked") -> the object still exists, the row is gone, and nothing durable names it. That is the exact unreconcilable-orphan state F4-3 claims to close; one best-effort writer can never be evidence that another best-effort writer succeeded. **The fix reuses an existing primitive and adds no table, queue, service, subsystem or migration:** the authoritative evidence write moved to `writeAuditLogInTx`, the non-swallowing audit writer already accepted for the security-critical bulk-export events, whose signature accepts any `Pick<PrismaClient, 'auditLog'>` so the global client satisfies it directly. **The invariant now enforced:** once the persisted row has been deleted, either (A) physical object deletion is terminally successful, or (B) a durable record carrying the reconciliation-safe object reference has committed — there is no silent third state. When neither holds, the result is reported as the new `outcome: 'evidence_persistence_failed'` (a value no caller can mistake for the tracked `failed`; `storageOutcome` still carries the storage-side truth and `evidence` reports whether the record committed), the condition is escalated to the process log as `UNEVIDENCED ORPHAN RISK` with the same PHI-safe object reference, and **both DELETE routes refuse to answer `success: true`** — they return `500` with `code: STORAGE_DELETE_UNEVIDENCED` and `recordDeleted: true`, stating the partial state truthfully without exposing the storage key or file name. The upload-rollback call sites no longer swallow their result either. **Scope honesty:** this guarantees the failure is either provably recorded or loudly reported as unrecorded; it cannot make a record durable while the database itself is unavailable, and it adds no automatic retry — `R-080` and `R-079` both stay **`OPEN`**. Proved behaviourally, not by source inspection: `storageDeletionEvidence.test.ts` §7 injects persistence failure at the Prisma delegate (10 new assertions; suite **23 -> 33**). Migration: still **NO**. Production mutation: still **NONE**. Full detail: [phases/F4_STORAGE_AND_BACKUP.md](phases/F4_STORAGE_AND_BACKUP.md) F4-3 section; [../compliance/53-kvkk-attachment-imaging-lifecycle.md](../compliance/53-kvkk-attachment-imaging-lifecycle.md) §16A.

29. **(Added 2026-08-16, F4-3-R2 — `R-079` closure PROPOSED, not claimed: the lab-attachment legal-hold gate. **Superseded the same day by item 30 below: `R-079` is now `CLOSED`.** As recorded at the time, `R-079` was `CLOSURE_PROPOSED_AWAITING_MERGE_AND_DEPLOYMENT` because PR #431 was still a draft and nothing was merged, deployed or production-verified. Smallest additive migration authorized by the program owner for `R-079` ONLY; no production mutation.)** Baseline `origin/main` @ `e1673f0be55d7413646353bdae26af47a2330dfe` (includes merged PR #430), clean tree. **What F4-3 left open, and why it mattered.** F4-3 and F4-3-R1 made the lab-order attachment deletion tenant-scoped and provable — they did **not** make it preventable. `LabOrderAttachment` carried no `legalHold` column, so `DELETE /api/lab-orders/:id/attachments/:attId` was the one physical attachment-delete path in the repository with **no legal-hold gate of any kind**, while `PatientAttachment` and `ImagingStudy` had had one since PR #160–#163. The concrete exposure: a lab attachment retained as a litigation or audit exhibit — an intraoral photograph sent to a technician — could be permanently destroyed by any holder of `LAB_ORDER_MANAGE_ROLES`, `RECEPTIONIST` and `ASSISTANT` included, while the equivalent patient attachment was protected. Under KVKK that is precisely the failure legal hold exists to prevent: special-category health data erased while an obligation to retain it is in force. **The schema delta is exactly two columns and one index** — `legalHold Boolean @default(false)`, `legalHoldReason String?`, `@@index([clinicId, legalHold])` — byte-for-byte the already-accepted `PatientAttachment`/`ImagingStudy` shape. Deliberately **not** added: `legalHoldAt`/`legalHoldById` (absent from the accepted contract; actor and timestamp live on the `AuditLog` row), `storageVerifiedMissingAt` (an orphan-inspection field — `orphanFileInspection.ts` walks `patientAttachment` and `imagingImage` only and never touches `labOrderAttachment`), and every retention field, lifecycle enum and deletion-intent table. **The invariant now enforced is a predicate, not a check:** the authorization decision is the single conditional `deleteMany({ id: attId, labWorkOrderId: id, clinicId: order.clinicId, legalHold: false })`. The route's pre-read survives, but only for metadata it cannot recover once the row is gone (`filePath` for the storage deletion, `originalName` for the activity log); it authorizes nothing. Postgres evaluates the predicate and performs the delete in one statement, so a concurrent legal-hold PATCH either commits first — zero rows affected, **neither the row nor the object touched** — or loses, in which case its own scoped `updateMany` affects zero rows and cannot resurrect a deleted row. `count === 0` is disambiguated **without widening tenant scope** (the re-read carries the identical ownership predicate): row gone → `404`; row present and held, including a hold that committed *after* the pre-read → `409 ATTACHMENT_LEGAL_HOLD` + audit; ownership mismatch → unreachable, already rejected upstream. **On the blocked path there is no DB delete, no physical storage deletion, and no storage-deletion evidence record claiming an attempt that never happened** — a recorded attempt that did not occur is as much a KVKK defect as an unprovable erasure. **Tenant ownership is unchanged** (`accessible clinic ids → LabWorkOrder → order.clinicId → LabOrderAttachment`); `req.user.clinicId` is the source of truth nowhere, and no mutation is ever issued against a bare attachment id. **No generic legal-policy framework was created.** None exists — `attachments.ts` and `imaging.ts` each own a separate per-domain PATCH endpoint — so the same precedent was followed: `PATCH /api/lab-orders/:id/attachments/:attId/legal-hold`, `authorize(['OWNER', 'ORG_ADMIN'])` taken verbatim from the accepted `PatientAttachment` contract (**no new role invented**, and deliberately narrower than the `LAB_ORDER_MANAGE_ROLES` set governing every other write on that router, because placing or releasing a hold is a legal act rather than lab coordination), a reason of at least 3 characters required in **both** directions, both directions audited, and the write itself a scoped `updateMany` carrying the full ownership predicate. `legalHoldReason` is redacted to `null` for every role except `OWNER`/`ORG_ADMIN` on all three read paths that return lab attachments and on the `409` body; the `legalHold` boolean is never redacted. The redaction helpers are a **local copy** rather than an import from `routes/attachments.ts`, matching what `routes/imaging.ts` already does — a route→route import would be the first cross-domain route dependency in the repository. **Audit/PHI:** the three new actions (`lab_order_attachment_legal_hold_set`/`_released`/`_delete_blocked_legal_hold`) carry no file name, patient name, TCKN, phone, email, DICOM metadata or reason text — only `entityId`, `labWorkOrderId` and the before/after boolean. **Backups are untouched and remain a separate question:** a legal hold on a primary row says nothing about pgBackRest repositories, `pg_dump` artifacts or `FileBackupRun` copies, and §16A's "primary object deletion is not backup deletion" applies unchanged in both directions. **Migration `20260816130000_add_lab_order_attachment_legal_hold` is expand-only** (`ADD COLUMN` ×2, `CREATE INDEX` ×1). Existing rows take the default `legalHold = false` — every attachment stays exactly as deletable as it is today, which is the only safe default, because a legal hold is an affirmative act recorded by an `OWNER`/`ORG_ADMIN` with a reason and back-filling one would fabricate a legal position nobody took. Validated on a disposable PostgreSQL 16: `prisma migrate deploy` exit 0, **75 migrations applied, unfinished 0, rolled-back 0**, `migrate status` "up to date", `information_schema` confirming `legalHold boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false` / `legalHoldReason text NULL` / `LabOrderAttachment_clinicId_legalHold_idx`, and `migrate diff --from-config-datasource` reporting **no residual difference relating to `LabOrderAttachment` or `legalHold`**. **Rollback is application-first** — revert the code and leave the additive columns in place, inert to anything that never reads them; dropping columns in production is **not** the immediate rollback path (§14's destructive procedure applies if they must ever go). **Proved behaviourally, not by source scan:** the new `test:lab-attachment-legal-hold` (**21/21**) drives the real Express route chain against real disposable objects on disk and includes a **TOCTOU hook** that commits a hold in the window between the metadata pre-read and the atomic `deleteMany`; `scripts/verify-attachment-legal-hold-lifecycle.ts` §6 (**23 → 34** assertions, real Postgres) adds a 20-trial race **and a forced lock interleaving** in which the DELETE is already blocked on the row lock when the hold commits, and under READ COMMITTED re-evaluates its predicate against the new row version to match zero rows — the exact point a read-then-delete implementation would destroy the held row. ## 13. Exact next task (Kesin sonraki görev)

**Exact next task, current for the EPIC F5 / queue-outbox lane (2026-08-22, set by F5-2R — Outbox Retention and Rollout Readiness).** This entry **supersedes the F5-3 lane entry immediately below it** for this lane only; every other lane stands unedited. Baseline `origin/main` @ `70ba73e0b2d3cc0b92462c281acba4619ad0d634` (PR #481 merge), fetched and verified at task start; both required merges confirmed as ancestors (`11956cf` = PR #480/F5-2, `70ba73e` = PR #481/F5-3). Branch `feature/f5-2r-outbox-retention-rollout-readiness`, cut from fresh `origin/main`, **not stacked** — ClickUp `F5-2R` ([`869enk93x`](https://app.clickup.com/t/869enk93x)).

- **What this closes.** The single rollout blocker F5-2 recorded against itself (§11 and §14 open item 1, and runbook rollout step 2): `OutboxEvent` and `OutboxConsumerExecution` were new persistent operational surfaces governed by **no** retention policy. **No F5-2 architecture was reopened** — the PostgreSQL outbox, in-process dispatcher, `SKIP LOCKED` claiming, versioned registry, replay-as-a-new-event and the idempotency ledger are all unchanged, and nothing under `server/src/outbox/` was modified except by the addition of one new file.
- **Three categories inside the EXISTING retention architecture, not a second framework.** `outboxProcessedEvents` (`status='processed'`, aged on `processedAt`, **180 days**, `DATA_RETENTION_OUTBOX_PROCESSED_EVENT_DAYS`), `outboxDeadEvents` (`status='dead'`, aged on `deadLetteredAt`, **365 days**, `DATA_RETENTION_OUTBOX_DEAD_EVENT_DAYS`) and `outboxConsumerExecutions` (`status='completed'`, **derived** window) are categories in `runDataRetentionCleanup`, using the existing `DataRetentionCategoryDeps` shape unchanged. No new scheduler, no new lock, no new entry point, **no new kill switch** — so `DATA_RETENTION_CLEANUP_ENABLED` and `privacy.dataRetention.runtimeEnabled` govern the outbox exactly as they govern the other nine categories, and a source-level test fails the build if a future `outboxRetentionJob.ts` tries to bypass them. The numbers are inherited rather than invented: 180 is the `OperationalEvent` window (a processed event is a discharged obligation whose residual value is diagnostics), 365 is the one-year family already used for conversation messages and resolved contact requests (a dead event is an obligation that was **not** discharged, and is the only object a replay can act on).
- **Nothing is deletable at any age in five states, and one of them is the interesting one.** `pending` and `claimed` events are undelivered obligations; `in_progress` and `ambiguous` executions are the duplicate-side-effect protection. The one that looks deletable and is not is **`claimed` with an EXPIRED lease** — that is not an abandoned row, it *is* the crash-recovery mechanism, and a sweep that "tidied up stale claims" would delete exactly the rows a dispatcher crash left behind. Every predicate pins `status` to an exact terminal literal, so widening a sweep to a protected state cannot be done without editing the file that documents why.
- **THE HIGH-RISK DECISION — the idempotency ledger — enforced twice, at two layers.** `replayDeadOutboxEvent` refuses with `ALREADY_APPLIED` by reading the **ledger**, not the event row (an event can be `dead` with the side effect already performed — that is what `AMBIGUOUS_SIDE_EFFECT` means), so a ledger row pruned ahead of its event would let a replay re-send a WhatsApp message the patient already received, silently, months later. **(1) In policy:** the consumer-execution window is `max(processed, dead)` and has **no environment variable** — every other window in `dataRetentionPolicy.ts` is a legitimate operator choice, this one is not, because a lower value is not a shorter retention period but a duplicate-patient-message defect with a several-month fuse. Deriving it makes the wrong value unrepresentable; a test proves none of the three plausible env-var names shortens it. **(2) Per deletion:** a `completed` ledger row is removed only once **no** event in `pending`/`claimed`/`dead` carries its `idempotencyKey` — which survives a hand-edited database, an errored category and a batch limit, none of which the policy layer alone survives. `processed` events deliberately do **not** pin the ledger (not replayable — `NOT_TERMINAL` — so they cannot cause a second side effect), tested in both directions. Two further guards make "dead events still required for unresolved operator action" a checkable predicate: an **open `ambiguous` marker** and an **in-flight replay descendant** each hold their dead event past its window, and each releases it once resolved/settled. Guards **fail closed** at a 10,000-row ceiling with the stable code `GUARD_SET_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a DLQ that large is an incident, and the worst moment to prune idempotency evidence is during one.
- **Dry run and batching.** `countEligible` is **the same predicate the delete uses, guards included**, so an operator is never shown a number the sweep would not act on (verified against a real database: a ledger row pinned by a dead event reports 0 eligible *and* deletes 0). Output is three integers — no payload, no organization/clinic/appointment id, no business key, asserted both DB-free and against a populated real table. A dry run performs zero mutations. Batches are bounded by the existing `DATA_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` and re-apply the full predicate in the delete, so a row that stops being eligible between select and delete is left alone; measured `2, 2, 1, 0` over five rows at `batchSize=2`, and repeat runs reach the same state with no over-deletion. Sweep order is events → ledger, and the invariant was tested by running the ledger sweep **first, out of order on purpose**, and watching the guard decline.
- **No migration.** `processedAt`, `deadLetteredAt`, `completedAt`, `status`, `idempotencyKey` and `causationId` already exist with the required meaning, and F5-2's `[status, …]` composite indexes serve the sweep. `MIGRATION_CREATED = NO`.
- **Tenant/KVKK.** Classification unchanged (`ORGANIZATION_SCOPED_DIRECT`, 28 tests green). The sweep is **deliberately global with no tenant predicate** — a retention job that could see one organization could not clean the table — and runs from the existing job, which establishes no tenant context, exactly as its nine existing categories do. **No new `SystemContextReason` (16 tests green), no raw SQL added (12 tests green, 21 files, zero `UNSAFE_BLOCKER`).** Nothing reads, selects, returns or logs `payload`; the module contains no `console.*` at all; `AuditLog` is untouched, so replay audit rows outlive the events they describe. `log-privacy-guard --strict-baseline`: 310 files, **no new violations**.
- **Tests: 59 new, 0 failed** — 32 appended to `test:data-retention` (48 → 80) and **27 in a new Layer 3 suite** `test:outbox-retention-db` against a real disposable PostgreSQL 16 with all 82 migrations applied. Eight existing suites re-run green (`outbox-contracts` 53, `auth`/`platformAdmin` 118, `retention-manual-run-audit` 29, `tenant-model-classification` 28, `raw-sql-tenant-audit` 12, `tenant-system-context-inventory` 16, `background-jobs-ownership` 10, `outbox-dispatcher-db` 43, `appointment-request-conversion-atomicity` 16, `messaging-inbound-reliability-db` 28). Server typecheck, frontend `tsc -b`, guardrail scan/tests and the log-privacy guard all clean. The three outbox/messaging DB suites were additionally re-run **in CI order on a freshly created database** (43 + 27 + 28, all green) to prove the new suite does not disturb its neighbours. **One honest observation:** the very first `outbox-dispatcher-db` run, against a database already used by two other suites, reported 42/1; the failing name was not captured and it did not reproduce in four subsequent runs including the clean-database CI-order run. Recorded rather than omitted — CI is the authority.
- **Operator verification surface.** `GET /api/platform/privacy/data-retention/policy` now returns `outboxProcessedEventDays`, `outboxDeadEventDays` and `outboxConsumerExecutionDays`, so rollout step "confirm retention is wired" can be performed without shell access and an operator can *see* that the derived window covers both event windows rather than take it on trust. No frontend change.
- **Rollout sequence for F5-2 is now documented end to end (runbook §1 + new §13) and was NOT executed.** Migration → application with both flags OFF → health → verify the policy recognises the outbox → verify both cleanup kill switches still gate it → optional dry run (all three counts are `0` on a fresh deploy, because no row can be 180 days old) → `OUTBOX_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true` → verify an empty drain → `OUTBOX_PRODUCER_ENABLED=true` → verify one controlled event → monitor `oldestPendingAgeMs`/`dead`/`staleLeases`. Rollback is unchanged and re-verified: producer OFF → drain → dispatcher OFF → revert; **never drop the tables**. Retention itself has no cutover to roll back — the runtime toggle, the env switch, or raising both outbox windows past every row's age each stop it, and there is nothing to un-delete because the sweep only ever removes rows that were already unable to do anything.

**Exact next task, current for the EPIC F5 / queue-outbox lane (2026-08-22, set by F5-3 — Messaging Fast-Ack, Retry/Backoff, DLQ and Replay).** This entry **supersedes the F5-2 lane entry immediately below it** for this lane only; every other lane stands unedited. Originally cut from `origin/main` @ `6e1d2e0b881a96f10aaf92d05984a7369448310b`; **restacked 2026-08-22 onto `origin/main` @ `11956cfcce37a56f5be2f9bb4e8b9e5340a50f35`**, which is the PR #480 (F5-2) merge commit. Branch `feature/f5-3-messaging-reliability-dlq-replay`, rebased — not merged — so it still carries the single F5-3 implementation commit plus the restack follow-up.

> **Overlap note — RESOLVED 2026-08-22.** The predicted textual conflict with the F5-2 PR happened and was resolved on this restack, additively, exactly as forecast. F5-2 merged first (PR #480); F5-3 rebased onto it. Three files conflicted — this §13, the F6 phase document and `server/package.json` (both tasks append test scripts) — and in every case **both tasks' entries survive**: the F5-2 lane entry stands verbatim immediately below this one, both change-history rows are present, and `server/package.json` runs the outbox **and** the messaging suites. Nothing was dropped and no F5-2 wording was rewritten. This mirrors the F5-1/F5-1P precedent recorded below.

- **NOT stacked on F5-2, and the reason is operational, not stylistic.** `.github/workflows/ci-pr.yml` triggers on `pull_request: branches: [main]` only, so a PR stacked onto the F5-2 branch would receive **zero checks** — no typecheck, no Layer 2/3/4/5, no guardrail — and `F5_3_CI_PASSED` could not be satisfied at all. F5-3 also needs nothing F5-2 introduced: its entire surface (`MessagingInboundEvent`, the retry job, three provider clients, two webhook routes) is on `main`, and it imports nothing from `server/src/outbox/`. **The cost was stated rather than hidden, and is now settled** — see the dedicated bullet below.
- **The duplicated retry vocabulary, re-examined now that F5-2 is on `main`, and resolved by halves.** The F5-3 PR recorded this as a follow-up on the assumption that the two vocabularies were “deliberately identical, so unification is a deletion”. Read against the merged F5-2 code that is **half true, and the honest half is the one that matters**. What is genuinely identical is the *arithmetic*: `computeBackoffMs` and `computeMessagingBackoffMs` were the same exponential-full-jitter computation line for line, differing only in which base table and which ceiling they read. That is domain-free, so it moved — one pure function in `utils/backoff.ts`, with both domains calling it and **neither importing the other**. What is **not** identical is the vocabulary itself, and the differences are real rather than cosmetic: messaging carries a `TIMEOUT` category the outbox has no way to raise (the dispatcher runs in-process — there is no socket to time out); the base delays differ by four to five times in every retryable category, because an inbound provider redelivery is a far slower loop than an in-process dispatch; the ceilings differ (30 minutes vs 1 hour); and the two persisted code unions share exactly **one** member out of seven each (`MAX_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED`) — the rest are `UNREGISTERED_EVENT`/`NO_CONSUMER`/`AMBIGUOUS_SIDE_EFFECT` on one side and `MISSING_CONNECTION`/`NO_RETRY_HANDLER`/`STUCK_IN_PROCESSING` on the other. Unifying *those* would mean handing one domain codes it can never emit, which is precisely the cross-domain coupling this lane exists to avoid, so **they are intentionally retained**, each in its own domain. The shared utility imports nothing, and there is no `outbox` → `messaging` or `messaging` → `outbox` import in either direction.
- **Re-scoped by F5-1/F5-1P evidence, as instructed.** `MessagingInboundEvent` is **preserved** as the single inbound durability ledger. No second ledger model, no Redis-only acceptance path, no BullMQ — all three asserted structurally by `tests/messagingReliability.test.ts`. Durable acceptance and provider dedupe were **not** rebuilt.
- **Four gaps were measured on `main` and closed.** (1) **Meta WhatsApp and Instagram sent their 200 BEFORE the durable ledger write** — a crash in that window loses the message permanently, and Meta never redelivers a webhook it has already 200'd. Evolution already had the right ordering. Now `validate -> durably accept/dedupe -> ACK -> process async`, with a **503** when acceptance itself fails so the provider's own retry becomes the backstop. (2) **`failed` meant four different things** — retryable, out of attempts, aged past the six-hour window (still `attempts: 1`, so it *looked* retryable forever), or from a channel the retry job never selects. Now `dead` + stable `lastErrorCode` + `deadLetteredAt`. (3) **Zero of 16 outbound `fetch` calls had a timeout**; a hung provider blocked a `withJobLock` lease and stalled every other clinic's reminders for that tick. Now bounded with a **ref'd** timer — deliberately **not** `AbortSignal.timeout()`, whose unref'd timer can leave a promise that never settles in a short-lived worker tick. (4) **A raw exception message was persisted** into `errorMessage`, and provider error strings are built by concatenating the provider's raw response body, which can echo a phone number or the message content. Now stable codes only.
- **Also delivered:** tenant-scoped DLQ inspection (no payload, no `errorMessage`, no phone number), bounded-cardinality platform metrics (status/channel/provider only), and bounded, audited replay that **reuses the row** — the opposite of F5-2's outbox replay, because an inbound event's identity is the provider's own message id and a second row would violate the dedupe constraint that makes the ledger work.
- **Deliberately NOT done, with triggers recorded.** No circuit breaker — §33 requires evidence of a retry storm, and **outbound has no retry at all today**, so there is nothing to storm; the trigger and the plumbing it would need are recorded. No automatic re-delivery handlers for Evolution/Instagram — that means re-running a conversational AI turn hours late, which is a product decision; their failures are now **visible and terminal** (`NO_RETRY_HANDLER`) instead of silently permanent. No outbox routing for outbound messages (§34: reminders are schedule-shaped). No operator HTTP route, so replay's *role* authorization is undecided by design. No ordering guarantees without evidence (§35).
- **Nothing is live.** One flag, `MESSAGING_DURABLE_ACK_ENABLED`, **default OFF**, exact-string `'true'`. Everything else ships unflagged because it makes an existing failure visible or bounds an existing call, and gating a strict improvement behind a flag nobody remembers to turn on is how a fix ships and never takes effect.
- **Tests: 77 new (49 DB-free + 28 against real PostgreSQL 16.14), 0 failed.** Seventeen existing suites re-run green, and the Meta/Instagram/post-booking webhook suites were re-run a **second time with `MESSAGING_DURABLE_ACK_ENABLED=true`** to prove the reordering itself. Two genuine defects were caught by these tests rather than by review: `parseRetryAfterMs('-5')` returned `0` instead of `undefined` (`Date.parse` reads `-5` as a year, silently turning a malformed header into "retry immediately"), and two `errorText` concatenations survived the first pass in `sendTemplateMessage` and `testConnection` — the latter being shown to clinic staff.
- **Migration `20260822130000_add_messaging_inbound_reliability_fields`** — six additive columns and one index; `nextAttemptAt` is NULL on every existing row, which is deliberately the pre-F5-3 meaning, so a database migrated ahead of the application behaves exactly as it does today. **Do not drop these columns on rollback** — `dead` rows would become indistinguishable from retryable ones and the replay audit trail would be destroyed.
- **Lifecycle:** `F5_3_AGENT_COMPLETED=YES` · `F5_3_TESTS_PASSED=YES` · `F5_3_PR_OPENED=YES` (draft) · **`MERGED=NO` · `MIGRATION_DEPLOYED=NO` · `APPLICATION_DEPLOYED=NO` · `FEATURE_ACTIVATED=NO` · `PRODUCTION_VERIFIED=NO`**.
- **One honest residual:** rows written before this change still hold raw exception text in `errorMessage`. F5-3 stops writing it and never reads it back, but does not rewrite history — a data migration over an operational column was judged the more dangerous option, and the existing `dataRetentionCleanupJob` sweep (which already covers `MessagingInboundEvent`) removes those rows on its normal schedule.
- **Exact next gate:** program-owner review and merge decision on the F5-3 PR (#481). F5-2 is already merged; F5-3 is restacked on it, CI re-run from scratch on the rebased head. **Exact next task, current for the EPIC F5 / queue-outbox lane (2026-08-22, set by F5-2 — Transactional Outbox and Versioned Event Registry).** This entry **supersedes the F5-1P lane entry immediately below it** for this lane only; every other lane stands unedited. Baseline `origin/main` @ `6e1d2e0b881a96f10aaf92d05984a7369448310b` (PR #479 merge), fetched and verified at task start. Branch `feature/f5-2-transactional-outbox-event-registry`, cut from fresh `origin/main`, **not stacked**.

- **The program-owner decision of 2026-08-22 changed the ADR statuses.** ADR-006 and ADR-007 moved `NEEDS_POC` → `ACCEPTED_WITH_CONDITIONS`. Current-stage mechanism: **PostgreSQL transactional outbox + in-process dispatcher**. **BullMQ/Redis DEFERRED** until a measured trigger (claim contention, throughput, delayed/repeat scheduling, multi-consumer fan-out, or another demonstrated operational trigger). ADR-006's acceptance is conditional: the outbox is authorized **only for genuinely outbox-shaped flows**, and is **not** authorization to migrate every cron/job. F6's entry condition ("ADR-006/007 kabulü") is therefore now `SATISFIED`; F6 moves `TODO` → `IN_PROGRESS`.
- **What F5-2 implemented.** Two additive models (`OutboxEvent`, `OutboxConsumerExecution`) in migration `20260822120000_add_outbox_event_and_consumer_execution`; a versioned event contract registry whose per-contract payload allowlist is enforced at publish **and** at dispatch, backed by a module-load net that refuses to import a contract permitting a PHI-shaped field name; a **transaction-only** producer (`publishOutboxEventInTx` takes a `Prisma.TransactionClient` first, so the commit-then-publish gap does not typecheck); a `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` claim with leases and crash recovery; category-driven bounded retry with full jitter; dead-lettering; audited replay that creates a **new** event with `causationId` and leaves the original `dead` as evidence; a business idempotency ledger with a real `UNIQUE (consumerKey, idempotencyKey)`; and per-organization backlog metrics.
- **One real flow, chosen on repository evidence.** All four F0-010 candidates were re-inspected. Appointment reminders and payment reminders are **schedule-shaped** (cron-derived, already ledgered via `SentMessage`, self-healing next tick); in-app notification generation is a **same-database idempotent `upsert`** whose correct fix is a transaction, not an event. The **appointment-request confirmation** is the genuine gap: `routes/appointmentRequests.ts` commits the conversion transaction, sends the HTTP response, then sends the patient's confirmation fire-and-forget with `.catch(log)` whenever the clinic has no external-calendar integration — a process exit or provider failure in that window loses it permanently with no record it was owed.
- **Nothing is live.** Two independent flags (`OUTBOX_DISPATCH_ENABLED`, `OUTBOX_PRODUCER_ENABLED`), both **default OFF**, exact-string `'true'` semantics. Deploying this branch changes no runtime behaviour. Rollout order is dispatcher-then-producer; rollback is producer-off, drain, dispatcher-off, and **never drop the tables**.
- **Tests: 96 new (53 DB-free contract + 43 against real PostgreSQL 16.14), 0 failed.** Fourteen existing suites re-run green, including `tenant-model-classification` (28), `raw-sql-tenant-audit` (12), `tenant-system-context-inventory` (16, with the new lock-free dispatcher job registered), and the conversion/outbound-sync atomicity suites **re-run a second time with `OUTBOX_PRODUCER_ENABLED=true`** to prove the cutover itself. Server typecheck, frontend `tsc -b`, architecture guardrail and the strict-baseline log-privacy scan all pass.
- **Lifecycle:** `F5_2_AGENT_COMPLETED=YES` · `F5_2_TESTS_PASSED=YES` · `F5_2_PR_OPENED=YES` (draft) · **`MERGED=NO` · `MIGRATION_DEPLOYED=NO` · `APPLICATION_DEPLOYED=NO` · `FEATURE_ACTIVATED=NO` · `PRODUCTION_VERIFIED=NO`**.
- **Open items that are rollout blockers, recorded rather than closed:** (1) `OutboxEvent`/`OutboxConsumerExecution` are new retention surfaces and are **not** yet in `dataRetentionCleanupJob`; (2) there is **no operator HTTP route** for metrics/DLQ/replay, so replay's *role* authorization is undecided by design; (3) tenant fairness is deliberately not implemented (F5-1P measured a naive cap making quiet-tenant latency five times worse) — the trigger is now measurable via per-organization backlog metrics; (4) ADR-006's volume projections remain genuinely unmet, pending production observability (ADR-012 `DEFERRED`).
- **Exact next gate:** program-owner review and merge decision on the F5-2 PR. Deployment stays gated on the retention item. > **Overlap note.** The F5-1 audit lane (PR #478, branch `docs/f5-1-queue-platform-authorization-audit`) edits this same §13 and the same F6 phase document. The two PRs are independent branches off `main` and **will conflict textually on the second merge**; the conflict is additive-only (two lane entries, two change-history rows) and both entries are intended to survive. Merge order does not matter.

- **Program-owner decision of 2026-08-22 (recorded in full by PR #478):** the F5-1 authorization audit was **ACCEPTED**; ADR-006 and ADR-007 stay `NEEDS_POC`; **BullMQ is NOT selected**; production rollout stays **NOT AUTHORIZED**; an **isolated/disposable PoC was explicitly authorized**. That authorization is the "separate, future task with its own review" required by [../architecture/queue-outbox-poc-design.md](../architecture/queue-outbox-poc-design.md) §12/§14. **F5-1P is that task, and it has now been executed.**
- **44 experiments, 44 PASS, 0 FAIL, 0 BLOCKED**, in throwaway Docker (PostgreSQL 16 / Redis 7.0), with `assertNoProductionEnvLeak()` refusing to start if a real connection string is present. No production system was contacted.
- **The decisive result is structural, not performance.** A BullMQ job **survives a rolled-back business transaction** (E11c: `waitingJobs: 1`, `appointments: 0` — an orphan event); the outbox closes exactly that gap (E11/E11b). Redis cannot enlist in a PostgreSQL transaction, so this is a property Candidate A has and Candidate B structurally cannot have alone.
- **Throughput is comparable once measured symmetrically:** 1,887/s (PostgreSQL) vs 1,684/s (BullMQ) at n=1000; 730/s vs 667/s at n=100. **A first run reported 21,277/s for BullMQ; that was a measurement artefact** (workers started before the enqueue loop, so the drain timed only the tail) and was corrected before the recorded run. The usual performance argument for BullMQ is therefore not currently supported at this scale.
- **A negative result is recorded rather than buried:** the naive per-tenant concurrency cap **made fairness worse** — quiet-tenant p50 rose from 292ms (no cap) to 1,962ms (cap=4), because the cap is applied *after* claiming and writes most of every batch back to `pending`. **Tenant fairness must be enforced at selection time, not after the claim.** Neither candidate gives fairness for free.
- **`MessagingInboundEvent` already provides what a large part of `F5-3` proposes to build** (M1): DB-enforced provider dedupe, retry state, all three inbound providers. The genuine remaining gaps are **DLQ inspection/replay tooling and queue metrics**, not durable acceptance. **`F5-3` should be re-scoped, not planned as new construction.**
- **Tenant safety proven against the REAL primitive** (`tenancy/tenantContext.ts` imported, not reimplemented): T1–T7 cover cross-tenant, sibling-clinic, missing/malformed identity, forged payload tenant id, concurrent duplicates and system-context misuse — all refused. No new system-context reason was required.
- **`ADR_007_RECOMMENDATION = B`** — PostgreSQL outbox + in-process dispatcher for the current stage, BullMQ deferred until a measured trigger (matching `queue-outbox-poc-design.md` §14 Stage 11). **This is evidence, not a decision: `ADR_007_FINAL_DECISION = PENDING_HUMAN_REVIEW`.**
- **Exact next task: the human ADR-007 architecture decision.** An agent cannot make it (§2.3). `F5-2` and `F5-3` stay `TO DO` behind it; `F6` phase stays `TODO`.
- **Explicitly NOT done:** no production rollout, cutover or migration; no production Redis/PostgreSQL contact; no Prisma migration (PoC schema sits outside `server/prisma/migrations/`); no change to `JobLock`, `MessagingInboundEvent`, `worker.ts`, any job, or any runtime path; `bullmq` added as a **devDependency only**, never imported by runtime code. Lifecycle: `AGENT_COMPLETED` / `TESTS_PASSED` / `PR_OPENED` — **`NOT_MERGED`, `NOT_DEPLOYED`, `NOT_PRODUCTION_VERIFIED`.**

**Pre-state (verified before any change):** `ufw status` → `inactive`. Public listeners (`ss -tulpn`) on the confirmed public IP (`curl ifconfig.me` → `94.138.221.64`, matching §7's RIPE-verified VPS2 identity) showed only `sshd` on `22/tcp` (v4+v6) plus loopback-only `systemd-resolved`/`chronyd`; no Docker, Postgres, Redis, or other service was publicly bound.

**Change applied:** `ufw default deny incoming`; `ufw default allow outgoing`; `ufw allow 22/tcp`; rules confirmed via `ufw show added` (single rule: `allow 22/tcp`) **before** enabling; then `ufw --force enable` (non-interactive, since UFW's interactive confirmation prompt cannot be answered over a scripted SSH command — the pre-enable rule-set check above is what makes this safe, not the prompt).

**Post-state (verified from a brand-new SSH connection, not a held-open session — session note below):** `ufw status verbose` → `active`, `Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), deny (routed)`, rules exactly `22/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere` + `22/tcp (v6) ALLOW IN Anywhere (v6)` — no other rule present. SSH login succeeded on the fresh connection. `docker ps` (Docker present, 0 containers running) confirms no container ports are exposed. `sshd_config`/`sshd_config.d` inspection shows `PermitRootLogin yes` and the pre-existing `Match User pgbackrest` block (from the prior VPS2-bootstrap task, §above) **unchanged** — this task touched only `ufw`, not `sshd_config`, so no human/operator SSH access path was altered.

**Session-model caveat:** the "keep the original session open, open a second and third independent session" procedure describes an interactive-terminal safety pattern; this agent's SSH access is a sequence of independent non-interactive `ssh host "cmd"` invocations (no held-open shell across tool calls), so "fresh connection" here means a new invocation issued after enable, which is what was actually done and verified above — recorded precisely rather than claiming a literal multi-tab session that did not occur.

**Rollback (not needed; verification passed, recorded per instruction):** `ssh noramedi-vps2-claude "ufw disable"` — returns the host to the verified pre-state (`inactive`, all ports reachable as before), reversible in one command, no reboot required.

**Scope:** firewall/network-policy only — no application code, no `sshd_config` change, no service installation, no data movement. Does not touch, advance, or close `R-030`/`R-030-DB`/`R-030-FILES`/`FIRST_CUSTOMER_RECOVERY_GATE`/`F4` phase status/GlitchTip, all of which remain exactly as recorded above (`OPEN`/`TODO`/`NOT_SATISFIED`/`DEFERRED`).

Continues the VPS2 imaging-storage-foundation work whose bootstrap/authorization record lives on `infra/vps2-bootstrap-f4-imaging-001-foundation` (PR #458, docs-only, `MERGED` into `main` 2026-08-19, merge commit `c9cfcb7` — see the two entries immediately above; that PR's `ROADMAP_ORDER_EXCEPTION = F4-IMAGING-001` grant, scope limits and `WHY_SAFE`/`DEPENDENCIES_NOT_BYPASSED` reasoning govern this task and are not re-derived here). This task is the "distinct, non-trivial coding task" that record scoped as its own follow-on, opened on its own branch (`feature/f4-imaging-001-vps2-storage-foundation`, off `origin/main`, not PR #458) with its own tests, per program-owner instruction.

**Architecture decision.** Evaluated three storage-transport options against the existing `fileStorage.ts` abstraction (local disk / `S3_BUCKET`-gated S3-compatible client, already used identically by patient attachments, lab attachments, imaging images and export archives) and the already-accepted `fileBackupDestination.ts` precedent (a second, independent S3-compatible destination in its own `FILE_BACKUP_S3_*` env namespace, with production HTTPS+SSE fail-closed enforcement):
- **Option A — S3-compatible object storage service on VPS2 (CHOSEN).** Reuses the AWS SDK S3 client/multipart-upload code paths the repository already depends on and already trusts (both `fileStorage.ts` and `fileBackupDestination.ts`); requires zero new application-level transport/retry/auth logic; fits `buildObjectStorageKey`'s existing `<clinicId>/<opaqueId><ext>` key contract with no key-shape change; is the natural precursor to any future Orthanc/DICOMweb object-storage architecture (explicitly not built now — see scope limit below). Implemented as a THIRD independent S3-compatible destination/env-namespace (`IMAGING_S3_*`, gated by `IMAGING_STORAGE_BACKEND=vps2`), following `fileBackupDestination.ts`'s exact validated shape (fail-closed config check before client construction, production-only HTTPS+SSE enforcement, explicit insecure/KMS overrides) rather than overloading the primary `S3_*` flag, because primary storage, off-host backup, and imaging-primary-on-VPS2 are three independently rotatable concerns (identical reasoning to why `FILE_BACKUP_S3_*` is already separate from `S3_*`).
- **Option B — purpose-built SSH/SFTP remote-storage adapter (REJECTED).** Would require inventing application-aware remote-filesystem code with no existing shape in this codebase (no `StorageObjectSpec`/`StoragePort` branch for it), duplicating transport/retry/streaming-upload logic the AWS SDK already provides for Option A, and would not reuse `buildObjectStorageKey`/`isSafeStorageKey`'s existing safety guarantees without new adapter-specific code. `pgbackrest`'s own repo2 SFTP account (VPS2 bootstrap work) is deliberately a "dumb storage endpoint" for a different subsystem (Postgres physical backup) and is not reused here — mixing an application-imaging write path onto the pgBackRest-only SFTP account would cross a boundary that VPS2 bootstrap intentionally kept separate.
- **Option C — mounted network filesystem / NFS (REJECTED).** No existing "remote filesystem" shape in `fileStorage.ts` (only local-path and S3-Key branches exist) — would require bypassing the local/S3 dichotomy entirely, the opposite of minimum change. Introduces a new failure-mode class this program has no operational experience with here (silent hangs/stale-handle errors under partition, no atomic multi-region write semantics, no native encryption-in-transit unless wrapped in a separate tunnel, no native versioning/lifecycle) and no per-object checksum/integrity story beyond whatever the mount layer happens to provide.

**Data-residency defect found and fixed fail-closed (the night's principal finding).** `validateImagingS3Config()` validated `IMAGING_S3_ENDPOINT` only `if (endpoint && ...)`, only under `NODE_ENV=production`, and only for its scheme; `getImagingS3()` then spread the endpoint in conditionally. So `IMAGING_STORAGE_BACKEND=vps2` with the endpoint **unset** passed validation and constructed an `S3Client` with no endpoint override — **the AWS SDK resolves its own default public AWS S3 endpoint.** Imaging objects (KVKK özel nitelikli sağlık verisi) would have been written outside Türkiye with no error, no log line, and the configuration still reading `vps2`. Same defect class as the accepted R1 enum correction: a configuration gap must never be indistinguishable from a deliberate, silently-different destination. **Fix:** new `resolveImagingS3Endpoint()` — endpoint required in EVERY environment when the backend is `vps2`, must parse as an absolute URL, must use `http:`/`https:`, production still requires `https://` unless `IMAGING_S3_ALLOW_INSECURE_ENDPOINT=true` (override semantics unchanged); `getImagingS3()` now passes `endpoint` unconditionally so no path can fall back. Deliberately DIVERGES from `fileBackupDestination.ts`, where an unset `FILE_BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT` legitimately means "use real AWS S3" — valid for a generic backup destination, invalid for a backend whose literal meaning is "the VPS2 host in Türkiye". Rationale recorded in the module header and `.env.example` so the asymmetry is not later "tidied up" into a bug. **+7 tests** (new section 2b). `IMAGING_S3_ENDPOINT_RESIDENCY_FAIL_CLOSED = IMPLEMENTED + TESTED`.

**Documentation-accuracy corrections (no behavior change).** (1) `.env.example` claimed VPS2 mode "REFUSES to start" — it does not; the only non-test caller of `validateImagingS3Config()` is `getImagingS3()`, so validation is **lazy, on first client construction inside a request**, with no boot-time call anywhere in `server/src`. (2) `.env.example` called the flag a "rollback switch" with no caveat; rollback is **one-way after the first VPS2 write**. Both corrected at the point an operator actually reads them.

- **(A) `IMAGING_BACKUP_COVERAGE_WHEN_VPS2_ACTIVE = BROKEN` — HIGH, blocking pre-activation gate.** `server/src/services/fileBackupService.ts` imports only the legacy `openFileStream` (`:40`), includes `ImagingImage` in `SOURCE_MODELS` (`:144`), reads at `:247`, and records `status: 'missing_source'` (`:258`). It was never rewired to `openImagingFileStream`. With the flag on, **every new imaging object is silently excluded from the off-host file backup** and logged as though the file were gone. Not listed in PR #459's touched-files record — an oversight, not a deliberate deferral.

**Finding (A) — the accepted merge blocker — is CLOSED.** `fileBackupService.ts` enumerated `ImagingImage` correctly through `imaging/ops.ts`'s `listImagesForBackup`, but opened the bytes of all three content classes through the single generic `openFileStream()`. Under `IMAGING_STORAGE_BACKEND=vps2` new imaging objects exist only in VPS2 object storage, so that read resolved `null` and the sweep recorded a healthy remote object as `missing_source` and never backed it up — a silent backup-coverage hole in the content class with the largest objects, labelled with the one status an operator would act on as data loss. The source reader is now selected per content class on the existing `SOURCE_MODELS` table: `PatientAttachment`/`LabOrderAttachment` keep calling `openFileStream()` unchanged, `ImagingImage` reads through `fileStorage.ts`'s `openImagingFileStream()` — the same VPS2-aware contract `routes/imaging.ts` already serves bytes from. Deliberately a re-use, not a re-implementation: no remote-client logic duplicated, Imaging domain boundary not bypassed, no direct Prisma access added, no new dependency edge (that module was already imported for `openFileStream`). Inheriting the contract supplies all three required semantics with no branch of its own — remote present → remote bytes; remote **confirmed absent** (404) + legacy present → controlled legacy fallback; remote **error** → throws, so the existing per-row catch records `failed`, never `missing_source` and never a silent legacy substitution. With the flag unset (production default) behavior is byte-identical to before. **Storage-key contract unchanged** (`<clinicId>/<opaqueId><ext>`, still `buildObjectStorageKey`); **`MIGRATION_REQUIRED = NO`**.

The minimal correct shape was designed — a nullable placement column (e.g. `storageBackend String?`, unset = legacy) populated on the write path and consulted on the read path — but that is a **schema migration plus write-path and read-path changes**, not the "small additive, fully tested" change authorized for this PR, and carrying a migration would make the merge decision materially riskier for no gain while the flag is off. `POST_FIRST_REMOTE_WRITE_SIMPLE_FLAG_ROLLBACK_SAFE = NO`. **`PRODUCTION_ACTIVATION_SAFE = NO` and must stay `NO` until (B) is resolved in its own accepted task.**

**Three pgBackRest findings recorded now rather than discovered during activation:** (1) `archive_command` must **not** carry `--repo` — `archive-push` writes to all configured repos and rejects the flag on 2.50 (`ERROR [031]`, observed live); (2) consequently **adding repo2 makes production WAL archiving depend on repo2 availability** — a repo2 outage fails `archive_command` on VPS1 and grows `pg_wal` until PGDATA fills, and `archive-push-queue-max` is currently **unset** in production, so it must be sized from `df -B1 $PGDATA` before activation; (3) never derive a `recovery_target_time` from a second-truncated timestamp — PostgreSQL stops before the first commit *after* the target, so a marker committed mid-second is itself excluded.

**GlitchTip upstream finding requiring a program-owner decision — cannot be closed by configuration.** In 6.2.6, `apps/users/utils.py` and `apps/organizations_ext/utils.py` evaluate `settings.ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION or not await User.objects.aexists()`, so on an instance with **zero users** registration and organization creation are open **regardless of the env vars**. Proven at runtime: on the freshly-migrated instance `GET /api/settings/` reported `enableUserRegistration: true` while the setting was `False`, an unauthenticated signup returned **200** and created user id 1, and that account then created an admin organization (**201**) — with both switches off. Once a user exists, signup returns **403** and organization creation **403**, verified by state (user count unchanged) and surviving a full restart. **Mitigation is procedural: the first superuser must exist before the port is reachable by anyone.** Also recorded: `ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION` **defaults to `True`** in this version (the original finding is confirmed); `ENABLE_SOCIAL_APPS_USER_REGISTRATION` is a separate, easily-missed setting; PII scrubbing is **off by default** (`ScrubConfig.enabled = False`) and a probe confirmed that with defaults, authorization headers, session cookies and synthetic special-category health fields landed **verbatim** in PostgreSQL; and `scrubIPAddresses` does not do what its name implies — it anonymizes only the server-observed connection IP and only when routable, so behind a proxy an SDK-supplied `user.ip_address` is stored verbatim. Explicit scrub configuration plus `ip_address` in `sensitive_keys` was applied and re-proven, and retention set to 7 days across event/transaction/file (`GLITCHTIP_EVENT_RETENTION_DAYS` alone leaves transaction and file retention at 90).

**Finding (B) — the accepted production-activation blocker — is CLOSED.** `model ImagingImage` recorded a storage *key* (`filePath`) but nothing about *which backend holds the bytes*, and that key is deliberately backend-independent — the same `<clinicId>/<opaqueId><ext>` string is used for local disk, legacy S3 and VPS2. Placement was therefore inferred at read time from the process-global `IMAGING_STORAGE_BACKEND`: all four routing decisions in `fileStorage.ts` were the same `isImagingRemoteStorageEnabled()` branch. After a first VPS2-only write, unsetting that flag silently reclassified those objects as legacy, made them unreadable, and made the backup sweep record them as `missing_source` — the one status an operator acts on as data loss. R6 adds an authoritative per-object discriminator, `ImagingImage.storageBackend String?` (nullable, **no default, no backfill, no new index**), and splits the two responsibilities that had been sharing one mechanism: **global configuration decides where NEW objects are WRITTEN; the row decides where an EXISTING object is READ from.** A `String?` and not a Prisma enum, matching this schema's convention for closed vocabularies (the schema has exactly one enum ever, added only alongside a brand-new table, and both recent closed vocabularies explicitly rejected enums — see `Patient.bloodGroup` and `20260819130000`). The two tokens `'legacy' | 'vps2'` are **reused verbatim** from the pre-existing `ImagingStorageBackend` type, aliased rather than redeclared, so there is one backend vocabulary and not two that can drift. The column holds a logical placement label only — never an endpoint, bucket, region, URL or credential, all of which stay in environment configuration.

**Read semantics (`resolveImagingStoragePlacement()` is the single authoritative interpreter, and every DB-row path funnels through it, so no two paths can disagree).** `NULL`/empty ⇒ `'legacy'`, meaning *"written before this column existed"*, resolved **deterministically and without consulting the flag** — a fact rather than a guess, because VPS2 imaging storage has never been activated in production, so no persisted row's bytes can be anywhere but legacy storage. `'legacy'` ⇒ legacy **only, even while the global write backend is `vps2`**. `'vps2'` ⇒ VPS2 **only**, including after the flag is unset; a confirmed-absent (404/`NoSuchKey`) response resolves `null`/`false` — a real "gone" — while any other provider error (network/auth/TLS/outage) **propagates**. Any unrecognized persisted value **throws** (fail closed): an unknown placement means the process does not know where the bytes are, and guessing would either serve the wrong object or report a healthy one as missing; in the backup sweep that surfaces as that row's `failed` entry, never `missing_source`, and never aborts the run. **There is deliberately no legacy fallback for an explicit VPS2 object, even on a confirmed 404** — R6 neither mirrors nor moves bytes, so a VPS2-placed object has no legitimate legacy twin, and serving whatever sits at the same key on local disk would return unverified bytes and hide real data loss behind a success. `isSafeStorageKey` still gates the remote path, so a pre-key-era absolute `filePath` is never sent to an object store as a key. **Corrected by the architecture-review fix entry below:** at the head this paragraph describes (`a5885819`), failing that gate under an explicit `'vps2'` placement silently fell back to legacy storage; it now fails closed. **Write semantics:** `saveImagingFile()` now returns the backend that actually accepted the bytes, produced on the same branch that performed the write, and `imagingIngestCore.ts` persists exactly that value — so "wrote to VPS2 but the row says legacy" and its converse are structurally impossible. The storage-write-then-transaction ordering and its best-effort compensation are **unchanged** (the storage/DB atomicity gap BLK-01 is pre-existing and was not widened); the compensation is strictly safer, because it now deletes from the backend the paired write used instead of re-reading the flag, which under R5 could have stranded the just-written object on the other backend as an untracked orphan.

**Every path that operates on an existing imaging object honours the discriminator** — stream/preview/download (`routes/imaging.ts`), exists/orphan reconciliation (`imaging/public.ts`'s `checkImageStorageExists`, consumed by `privacy/orphanFileInspection.ts` — without this it would have stamped `storageVerifiedMissingAt` on healthy VPS2 rows), backup source read and backup enumeration (`fileBackupService.ts` + `imaging/ops.ts`), and the ingest compensation delete. A structural Layer 2 guard (`imagingStoragePlacementCallSites.test.ts`) asserts that no production module outside `fileStorage.ts` consults the global flag for routing, that no module outside the imaging domain imports the provider module, and that placement never reaches a response body. Paths deliberately out of scope, each with the reason it cannot misroute storage, are recorded in the evidence §7: KVKK patient/clinic export and deletion-review read **metadata only and never imaging bytes**; anonymization redacts `originalName` and never touches storage; backup restore reads from the backup **destination**, not primary storage.

**Backup contract preserved and extended, R5 Finding (A) not regressed.** Enumeration still goes through `imaging/ops.ts` (no direct Prisma access reintroduced — pinned by `fileBackupImagingOpsPortMigration.test.ts`), bytes still open through the Imaging-owned reader, no provider logic duplicated, destination key shape unchanged. The `ImagingBackupRow` DTO allow-list widens by **exactly one** field, the raw `storageBackend` column, which the sweep interprets through the single authoritative resolver **at the point of use rather than during enumeration** — a blast-radius decision, not a stylistic one: the resolver fails closed, and the sweep's per-row `try`/`catch` begins after the `for await` step, so interpreting during enumeration would let one unclassifiable row abort the whole sweep and silently stop backing up every imaging row after it, instead of producing that single row's `failed` entry while everything else is still backed up. The allow-list stays closed against study metadata/modality/patientId/originalName, and a structural test asserts the interpreter does not appear inside the enumeration generator. NULL/pre-R6 and explicit-legacy rows back up from legacy; an explicit VPS2 object backs up from VPS2 **including after a flag rollback**; a VPS2 provider error is `failed`, never `missing_source` and never silently satisfied from a same-key legacy object; `PatientAttachment` and `LabOrderAttachment` are unchanged.

**A defect in R6's own tests, found by the rebase and fixed.** The rebase re-materialized `schema.prisma` from Git, which on this Windows checkout means **CRLF** — and two new assertions extracted the `model ImagingImage` block with an `indexOf` anchor containing a bare LF-brace-LF sequence, which never matches under CRLF. `indexOf` returns `-1`, `slice(start, -1)` returns almost the whole file, and the consequences differed: the "index set is exactly `[clinicId, studyId]`" check failed loudly, listing every index in the schema, while the "declares `storageBackend String?`, no credential-shaped field" checks had been **passing vacuously** against the entire file. Both now use a line-ending-tolerant search plus an explicit `block.length < 3000` guard, so a future regression to whole-file matching fails loudly instead of silently. Stated plainly because it matters: **CI runs on Linux with LF and would never have caught this** — under LF the anchor matches, so the loud half would have been green and the vacuous half would have stayed green forever; it surfaced only because this task happened to rebase onto a fresh checkout mid-session. The same bare-LF `indexOf` idiom exists in the pre-existing `kvkkAttachmentImagingLifecycle.test.ts` schema assertions and carries the same latent weakness; reported, not changed here. **Four existing pinned contracts legitimately changed and were updated with their rationale in-source, never loosened or deleted:** the `fileStorage.ts` wrapper arity assertions moved from `1` to `2` (TypeScript emits an optional parameter as a plain one, so this genuinely moved rather than passing silently — and a new case now pins the added parameter by signature *and* behavior, proving it is the closed two-token placement union and structurally cannot carry a tenant id); the `ImagingBackupRow` DTO allow-list gained `storagePlacement`; the ingest compensation assertion now requires the placement-carrying form and forbids the placement-less one; and `fileBackupDbIntegration`'s `createImagingRow` takes an explicit placement — **every assertion in that suite is unchanged**, its VPS2-only fixtures simply now carry the `'vps2'` value the production write path actually persists.

**Security / tenant / KVKK.** Storage placement is not authorization and is never used as one — placement is read *from an already tenant-scoped row*, so it cannot widen access. Cross-tenant denial is now positively tested against the new column for **both** placement values, and the test proves the tenant predicate runs **before** any storage lookup by pointing the endpoint at an unreachable address and asserting a `NotFound` rather than an unavailable error. Placement is server-derived, written once at ingest, and never read from request input (asserted for both the tenant and bridge routes); it never reaches a response body (`studyImageSelect` and the cross-domain lifecycle DTO both asserted clear, per docs/compliance/53 §10). Every R3/R5 fail-closed configuration rule stands untouched — `IMAGING_S3_ENDPOINT` required in every environment under `vps2`, `endpoint:` passed unconditionally, scheme/HTTPS/SSE validation, fail-closed unknown backend — and **no public AWS fallback was introduced**. No new logging; the placement is not logged and no storage key is logged; the log-privacy baseline lines were not reworded. No credential value appears in source, tests, evidence, tracker or PR body. **`storageBackend = 'vps2'` records where bytes live and is explicitly NOT a claim about encryption at rest, SSE, residency evidence or provider approval.**

**Backward compatibility, and the one deliberate behavior change, stated rather than buried.** Pre-R6 rows keep `NULL` and read as legacy; old absolute-path `filePath` rows are unaffected; the previously deployed release never references the column and, because it is nullable with no default, every INSERT that release performs stays valid; the storage-key contract is unchanged and **no byte was moved and no key rewritten**; attachments and export archives are untouched. The change: under R5 a placement-less row was probed against VPS2 first whenever the flag was on, and under R6 it reads legacy directly. For production this is a no-op — the flag has never been on there. For a **non-production environment that activated VPS2 before R6 and still holds rows written in that window**, those rows now read as legacy until their `storageBackend` is set to `'vps2'` (a one-line `UPDATE` on a staging database). That is the necessary price of determinism: a rule that still depended on the flag would not survive a config rollback, which is the entire defect R6 removes.

**Rollback.** *Pre-activation:* safe — the column is inert to code that never reads it, and application rollback needs no schema change. *Post-first-VPS2-write:* rolling back the **write flag** is now safe, which is the point of R6 — but **(a)** the `IMAGING_S3_*` connection settings must **stay configured**, because VPS2-placed objects are still read from VPS2, and removing them fails closed with an explicit configuration error rather than silently falling back to legacy (deliberate: serving whatever sits at the same key on legacy storage would be worse than failing); **(b)** the column must **not** be dropped — it is then the only record of where those bytes are, and dropping it destroys the placement evidence and recreates exactly the failure R6 prevents; roll back *application activation*, not the schema; **(c)** do not revert to a release that ignores placement unless every VPS2-placed object is provably reachable under the old configuration, which for a VPS2-only object it is not; **(d)** physically decommissioning VPS2 remains a data migration, not a config change. **`POST_FIRST_REMOTE_WRITE_SIMPLE_FLAG_ROLLBACK_SAFE = YES`**, conditional on (a).

**Boundary discipline: R6 added no new cross-domain edge, and avoided the one it was most tempted into.** `routes/imaging.ts` and `fileBackupService.ts` must interpret a persisted placement value; importing `resolveImagingStoragePlacement` straight from `imagingRemoteStorage.ts` would have created a route→provider-internals edge and a Core→provider-internals edge onto a module the guardrail cannot even attribute an owner to. Instead `fileStorage.ts` **re-exports** the resolver and both import it from there — their accepted dependency (`CDA-009`) which they already had. It is a re-export, not a second implementation; the interpreter stays singular, and a structural test asserts the only importers of `imagingRemoteStorage.js` are `fileStorage.ts` and the imaging domain itself, and that neither the route nor the sweep touches a provider primitive or the global flag. **Two pre-existing boundary items reported, deliberately NOT fixed here** (R6 is not a refactor): (1) `server/src/services/imagingRemoteStorage.ts` is absent from the architecture guardrail's `domain-map.json`, so its inbound edges classify as `UNRESOLVED`; introduced by this lane before R6, gates nothing today (the guardrail is report-only), and needs a deliberate ownership decision rather than a drive-by line. (2) `routes/imaging.ts`'s byte-path `findFirst` scopes on `study.clinicId` only, not also on `ImagingImage.clinicId` as `imaging/public.ts` does — a denormalization mismatch would go undetected and mis-attribute the audit entry; **not exploitable through the API** (no path can create such a mismatch) and not made worse by R6; recommended fix for its own task. **One CI-classification correction was made**, because it concerns the exact file R6 modifies: `scripts/ci-classify/classify.ts` did not list `imagingRemoteStorage.ts` among the storage service files, so a PR touching only that file fell through to `BACKEND_GENERAL` and would have **skipped the Postgres and storage-integration layers that actually exercise it**. R6 itself was never at risk (it touches `schema.prisma`, which forces the full gate); the fix only widens coverage. A stale, sentence-spliced R3 "TIMING CAVEAT" paragraph in `server/.env.example` — which asserted no boot-time `validateImagingS3Config()` call existed, made false by R5's Finding C — was also corrected, alongside the now-superseded "rollback is one-way after the first VPS2 write" paragraph.

**Exact next task, current (2026-08-20, F4-IMAGING-001-R6-R1-PLACEMENT-FAIL-CLOSED-REVIEW-FIX — architecture-review fix on the SAME PR #464).** Not a new task lane and not a new PR: this is the architecture review of PR #464 (item (1) of the R6 entry's "exact next task") coming back with one accepted finding, fixed on the same branch `feature/f4-imaging-001-r6-storage-placement-discriminator`. Reviewed head was `a58858195867011c650f278b11d04c21091d6532`, confirmed unmoved before any edit. **No VPS1/production access was used, requested, or required. No real patient/DICOM/CBCT data, no production DB dump and no production backup was touched. `IMAGING_STORAGE_BACKEND` was not changed outside disposable test processes. Nothing was merged, deployed or activated, and no VPS2 activation is claimed.** Evidence: §14 of `docs/program/evidence/F4-IMAGING-001-R6_STORAGE_PLACEMENT_DISCRIMINATOR_EVIDENCE.md`.

**The finding, accepted in full.** R6's design is correct — `'vps2'` ⇒ VPS2 only, `'legacy'` ⇒ legacy only, `NULL` ⇒ legacy, unknown ⇒ fail closed — but the implementation did not hold it in one corner. `openImagingFileStream`/`imagingFileExists` branched on `placement === 'vps2' && isSafeStorageKey(ref)` and fell through to `openFileStream`/`fileExists` for **every** other case, while `deleteImagingFile(key, 'vps2')` routed to VPS2 with no key gate at all. So for one and the same object — a row explicitly recorded `'vps2'` whose `filePath` cannot be an object-storage key (absolute path, UNC/drive path, traversal segment, control character) — **read said legacy, exists said legacy, delete said VPS2.** The read arm is the worst of the three: it hands back whatever unrelated bytes happen to sit at that local path *as the VPS2 object*. The exists arm returned a legacy-derived "confirmed absent" for a row that says the bytes are on VPS2 — exactly what makes the orphan sweep stamp `storageVerifiedMissingAt` on a healthy row. **Root cause:** `isSafeStorageKey` was used as a *routing* condition when it is a *validity* condition on the row; falsifying a routing condition selects the other backend, falsifying a validity condition means no backend can be selected honestly. **Reachability, stated honestly rather than inflated:** today's production code cannot produce this combination (`saveImagingFile()` only ever receives a `buildObjectStorageKey()` result, and `'vps2'` is written only by the write that stored the bytes), so this is fixed as a correctness/consistency defect and not as a live incident — but a hand-edited row, a partial restore, a future backfill or an import all reach it, and a placement discriminator that is not trustworthy under exactly those conditions is not worth having.

**The fix — minimum change, no new layer, no refactor.** One sanitized error type and one gate helper in `fileStorage.ts`; the three explicit-`'vps2'` branches call the gate first. `ImagingPlacementRefMismatchError` (`code = 'IMAGING_PLACEMENT_REF_MISMATCH'`, fixed-literal message, no ref/key/bucket/endpoint/region/credential/patient data in the message or in the throw-site log line, which prints the code only). It is a **throw**, never a `null` and never a `false`: "I cannot tell where these bytes are" must not be indistinguishable from "this object is genuinely gone". **Delete is gated too, deliberately** — fixing only read/exists would have left the mirror image of the same disagreement. No caller changed: the route's existing outer `catch` returns its sanitized 500; `checkImageStorageExists` wraps it in the facade's own `ImagingStorageUnavailableError`, which propagates out of `inspectOrphans()` (it does not catch per row) and fails the inspection instead of classifying the row `dbRowPhysicalMissing`, so `markConfirmedMissing()` is never handed it and `storageVerifiedMissingAt` is never stamped; the backup sweep records that row as `failed` with `errorMessage = 'IMAGING_PLACEMENT_REF_MISMATCH'` via `safeErrorFields`, never `missing_source`, never aborting the run. **Backward compatibility is unchanged in every direction that matters:** `'legacy'` reads pre-key-era absolute paths exactly as before, `resolveImagingStoragePlacement(NULL) === 'legacy'` so every pre-R6 row stays readable, and the omitted-placement compatibility seam was neither broadened nor redesigned — the gate applies only to an *explicit* `'vps2'`. Production DB-row call sites still pass explicit placement, still pinned structurally.

**Migration: comment wording only. No new migration, no structural change.** `20260820130000_add_imaging_image_storage_backend`'s header claimed the operation was "catalog-only … a brief `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, no table rewrite, and a duration independent of row count. Safe on the production `ImagingImage` table at any size." The no-rewrite assessment is correct for a nullable `ADD COLUMN` with no default on supported PostgreSQL and is unchanged; the wording bounded how long the lock is *held* and then read that as a bound on the whole statement. It now states precisely: no table rewrite; row-count-independent execution work **after lock acquisition**; a brief `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock is required; **acquiring it can wait** behind concurrent/long-running transactions (`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` conflicts with `ACCESS SHARE`, so even a long read blocks it, and everything else then queues behind the waiter); and **the production deploy must abort/stop if the migration cannot acquire its lock within the operator-approved migration window/timeout.** No session `lock_timeout`/`statement_timeout` was added — no existing migration in this repository issues a `SET`, so there is no accepted convention to follow, and putting a production timeout policy in this one file would hide it from the operator running `prisma migrate deploy`. **The directory name, timestamp and the single `ALTER TABLE` statement are byte-identical to `a5885819`**; only `--` comment lines changed, and the §4 pinning test strips comments before asserting. No R10 artifact was read for content, renamed, reordered, edited, or given a changed timestamp; no `schema.prisma` change was needed or made.
